title: Ms. Blakk for President by Tarell Alvin McCraney and Tina Landau at V...
transcript: “If a bad actor can be president, why not a good drag queen?” This immersive new production at Vineyard tells a piece of queer history that's unknown to many and almost as outlandish as our modern political climate. After a decade of inaction and indifference from the powers that be during the AIDS epidemic, drag artist Terence Alan Smith and other members of Queer Nation were advocating for mainstream queer visibility and meaningful acknowledgement from the government. And what better way to kickstart a national platform than with a presidential campaign? Written by Oscar winner Tarell Alvin McCraney and Tony nominee Tina Landau, who also directs the piece, Ms. Blakk for President is a rapturous retelling of a remarkable story, carrying the passion, joy, and resistance that made the story possible. Much of it is narrated in direct address by Terence/Joan, played by Ato Blankson-Wood in maybe my favorite performance of his to date. His Joan is sharp and ferocious, rolling poetry off of her tongue as easily as her witty and dirty jokes. The piece seamlessly intertwines drag, narrative, crowd work, and music, and even at just a hundred minutes long, it manages to invoke a lot of ideas around activism and audacity in the face of apathy. The production design is gorgeous, completely transporting you to the underground queer club scene of the 90s — the musical selections certainly help with that. The script is efficient, as is the staging, but it felt strangely sparse to me, considering how well-paced it is and how much they've decked out the theatre. Maybe it's something about the small cast size or the layout of the room, but the scale didn't feel quite right to me, and the moments of euphoria hit a ceiling as a result. Don't get me wrong, it still brought some euphoria, but maybe it would hit even harder in a larger venue. That said, I am glad it's being produced right now. The way it touches on how activism isn't a straight line, that it's sometimes hard to agree on how to fight the fight even when you have a common goal, feels especially relevant today. Winning the presidency was Queer Nation's last priority — the point was to make noise, raise awareness, and live radically by living joyfully.
reasoning: Creator praises the writing, performance, and relevance enthusiastically but notes a clear caveat about scale and euphoria hitting a ceiling. Lands as a strong positive recommendation rather than a full rave.
